title: Washing feet

lines: A TOWEL, A BASIN, SOME WATER.
cards: A towel, a basin, some water: that's the whole scene's equipment.
It's the last supper Jesus shares with his friends before his arrest, in John's Gospel, and the room is full of people who have walked dusty roads in sandals. Partway through the meal, he gets up.

He takes off his outer garment, ties the towel around his waist, pours water into the basin, and kneels in front of the first pair of feet. The room goes quiet. One of them is about to object, loudly.

teach.b: John opens the scene with love: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Then, instead of a speech, a chore. First, whose job this was.

When Abigail agrees to marry David in First Samuel, she says, "let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." In her words, it's the task of a servant who serves the servants. Second, Peter.

teach.h: THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.
teach.b: He can't stand it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers him, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter, being Peter, swings the other way: then not just my feet, but my hands and my head.
Letting yourself be served turns out to be its own kind of humility. Third, who gets washed.
The text says Jesus knew who would betray him, and readers notice no one is skipped: Judas's feet were in that room too.
Fourth, the instruction: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet."

teach.h: I HAVE GIVEN YOU AN EXAMPLE.
teach.b: And: "I have given you an example." Churches take that in different ways.

Some, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican among them, wash feet in a service on the Thursday before Easter; some smaller churches do it whenever they share communion; others read it as a picture of everyday service rather than a rite.
The gesture at the center stays the same: love that kneels down.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and some other churches hold a foot-washing on the Thursday before Easter, and some smaller churches wash one another's feet as part of communion.

o: a way to welcome kings to a royal feast
a servant's chore Jesus did to show love
a cleansing rite before entering the Temple

s: Peter happily lets Jesus wash his feet
he refuses first: thou shalt never wash my feet. then asks for his hands and head too.
washing feet was a servant's job in the old stories
Abigail offers to be a servant to wash the feet of David's servants.
every church turns foot-washing into a service

games.q: you're Peter. your teacher is kneeling in front of you with a towel and a basin. what do you say?
o: thank you, and put your feet out.
thou shalt never wash my feet.
nothing; you pretend it isn't happening.
games.why: Peter refuses, until Jesus says, if I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me. then he asks for his hands and head too.

practice: Look down at your own feet for a moment, then let a person come to mind whom you could serve in a small, low, unglamorous way: the dishes no one wants, the heavy bag, the boring shift.
Picture yourself doing it without announcing it. Then notice whether there's someone you've refused to let serve you, and if you pray, bring both to God in a few plain words.

wordCard.voice: Washing feet. In John's Gospel, Jesus takes a servant's job at his last supper and tells his friends to do the same for one another. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to wash the feet, the phrase John uses for what Jesus began to do.

carryVoice: Your line: wash feet. Love that kneels, and lets itself be served. That's day eight hundred thirty-two.
